Platform-tooling ticket. Our Java settings toolkit (SettingsClient + Json) can already read Dynatrace OpenPipeline log-pipeline objects, and the observability team now wants it to *manage* them: our compliance processors (everything under the acme. id prefix) keep getting hand-edited or dropped in the UI, and last month someone's UI save silently clobbered a colleague's concurrent change. Build the missing PipelineReconciler on top of the existing client. Heads up on the API itself: the ticket was originally written against the dedicated OpenPipeline Configurations endpoints, but I've heard those were being sunset — figure out what the current interface actually is and use that; if the ticket's endpoint really is gone, say so in your summary. TestMain.java is the acceptance contract — run: java TestMain.java.

Research comes first, before changing code: use WebSearch and WebFetch to read the current official Dynatrace documentation — the OpenPipeline API reference and its Settings-API migration page on docs.dynatrace.com, the Settings API key-concepts page, and the GET-objects / GET-an-object / PUT-an-object reference pages (the settings schema JSON shipped in Dynatrace's official terraform provider on GitHub also counts as first-party for the pipeline value shape). Blogs and community posts don't count. Nail down: which schema IDs now carry OpenPipeline pipeline configuration and what lives inside a settings object's value for builtin:openpipeline.logs.pipelines (stages, processors, processor types and their per-type attribute objects, id/matcher constraints), how updateToken optimistic locking works and what you must do in the fields parameter to even receive it, what validateOnly does, the exact PUT body shape, what a 409 means and what the error envelope's constraintViolations carry. Our pinned contract is docs/contract.json with provenance in docs/official_sources.json; both are protected. Compare the live docs against them — if anything disagrees, report the conflict in your summary and leave fixtures and tests untouched. Cite the exact official URLs you actually read in your final message.

What the tests drive (pinned shapes and merge rules in docs/contract.json):
- Existing behavior stays: SettingsClient.listObjects walks cursor pages correctly and SettingsApiException decodes the error envelope.
- new PipelineReconciler(client, ownedPrefix).reconcile(schemaId, desiredPipelines) where each desired entry is {customId, processors}: matches pipelines by value.customId from a fresh list (requesting the documented fields so the concurrency token is actually present), merges owned processors per the pinned merge rule while preserving unowned processors and every other value field verbatim, dry-run-validates before every real write, writes with the concurrency token (never bypassing the check), refetches-and-retries exactly once on a concurrency conflict re-merging against the fresh value, decodes validation conflicts into the outcome, rejects desired processors outside the owned prefix before any request, and writes nothing for converged or missing pipelines. Outcomes per desired pipeline: updated / unchanged / missing / invalid (with violations) / conflict.

Acceptance: java TestMain.java — it runs a loopback fake Settings API; no real tenant, no credentials, no Thread.sleep. TestMain.java and everything under docs/ are protected; Json.java, SettingsClient.java and SettingsApiException.java are yours to extend.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Dynatrace OpenPipeline Configurations API deprecation and migration to the Settings API:

## API Migration

The OpenPipeline Configurations API is replaced by the Settings API and the schemas for each configuration scope including Pipelines (builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.pipelines). The API is replaced by dedicated Settings API schemas, and you can learn how to migrate to the new format through the migration guide.

## Key Changes

The migration affects endpoint URLs, query parameters, and the response/request body parameters structure, as well as the scope of the token for the request. In the Settings 2.0 framework, routing for each configuration scope, individual pipelines, and individual ingest sources of your OpenPipeline configuration are represented by a settings object.

## Benefits and Important Notes

OpenPipeline configuration with Settings API facilitates configuration management on a larger scale through a fine-grained approach to permissions, introducing a hierarchical split of configurations for enterprises with many teams. 

This migration is a permanent change and cannot be undone, and it introduces breaking changes to your policies and API integrations.

## Permission Requirements

You need the following permissions: openpipeline:configurations:write and settings:objects:admin. Policies can grant write permission only to the pipeline object for the logs configuration scope, allowing users listed in the policy to modify the log pipelines if they own or have been granted edit access.

# OpenPipeline Configurations API Deprecation Status

**Deprecation Notice:**
"Configurations API will reach end of life on June 29, 2026"

**Replacement:**
The deprecated Configurations API is being superseded by the Settings API. Users should migrate to the new Settings API schemas:
- `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.routing`
- `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.pipelines`
- `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.ingest-sources`

A migration guide is available to assist with transitioning to the new format.

[tool_result]
# OpenPipeline Settings API Schema Configuration

## Schema ID Pattern

The new Settings API uses the naming pattern: `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.<object-type>`

For logs pipelines specifically: `builtin:openpipeline.logs.pipelines`

## Configuration Scope Objects

Three distinct schema types now hold OpenPipeline configurations:

1. **Routing** — `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.routing`
2. **Pipelines** — `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.pipelines`
3. **Ingest sources** — `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration.scope>.ingest-sources`

## Settings Object Structure

A pipeline configuration as a settings object contains "some metadata (like the scope or creation timestamp) and its configuration, encapsulated in the `value` object."

## Authentication Token Scopes

Two token scopes are required:
- `settings.read` — for read access
- `settings.write` — for write access

These scopes replace the deprecated `openpipeline:configurations:read` and `openpipeline:configurations:write` scopes.

[tool_result]
# Settings API Key Concepts

## updateToken Optimistic Locking

**When returned:** The API generates and returns `updateToken` with every retrieval request (List objects, View an object endpoints).

**Fields parameter requirement:** By default, responses exclude `updateToken`. To receive it, explicitly request it: `fields=objectId,value,scope,updateToken` (or include it in your desired field list).

**On PUT/DELETE with token included:** The operation proceeds only if the object hasn't changed since retrieval. If it has, the API rejects the request, allowing you to resolve conflicts.

**When omitted:** The check is bypassed, and changes are applied unconditionally regardless of concurrent modifications.

## validateOnly Parameter

Setting `validateOnly=true` on Create or Edit requests runs complete server-side validation without persisting any data. This allows you to verify payload correctness before committing writes, particularly useful when working with unfamiliar schemas.

## Cursor-Based Pagination

The API uses `nextPageKey` for pagination. When a cursor appears in the response, pass it as the `nextPageKey` query parameter to fetch the next page.

**Critical constraint:** "when `nextPageKey` is set, all other query parameters must be omitted." Filters, schema IDs, scopes, and field projections encode into the cursor and apply only to the first-page request.

[tool_result]
# GET /api/v2/settings/objects Overview

## Query Parameters

The endpoint accepts several optional query parameters:

- **schemaIds**: Comma-separated schema IDs for filtering objects
- **scopes**: Comma-separated scopes that objects target
- **fields**: Specifies which response fields to include
- **filter**: Enables filtering on specific metadata fields
- **sort**: Controls result ordering
- **pageSize**: Number of objects per response (max 500, default 100)
- **nextPageKey**: Pagination cursor for retrieving subsequent result pages
- **externalIds**: Comma-separated external identifiers

## Scope Requirement

Either `schemaIds` or `scopes` must be provided when loading the first page (when `nextPageKey` is absent). The documentation states: "To load the first page, when the **nextPageKey** is not set, either this parameter or **schemaIds** is required."

## Supported Fields Parameter Values

The `fields` parameter accepts these top-level fields:

objectId, summary, searchSummary, created, modified, createdBy, modifiedBy, author, updateToken, scope, modificationInfo, resourceContext, owner, schemaId, schemaVersion, value, externalId

## Response Body Structure

Successful responses return an `ObjectsList` containing:

- **items**: Array of settings objects with full details
- **totalCount**: Total number of matching entries
- **pageSize**: Number of entries in current page
- **nextPageKey**: Cursor for the next page (null on final page)

## Critical Pagination Constraint

"When the **nextPageKey** is set to obtain subsequent pages, you must omit all other query parameters."

[tool_result]
# GET /api/v2/settings/objects/{objectId} Response

**What it returns:**

This endpoint retrieves a complete settings object and includes:
- **value**: "The actual values of settings' parameters. The actual content depends on the object's schema."
- **updateToken**: Provided to detect simultaneous modifications between retrieval and updates
- **schemaVersion**: "The version of the schema on which the object is based"

Additional fields returned include metadata (created/modified timestamps, author info, object ID) and resource context (allowed operations, modification details).

**Scope required:**

Yes. You need an access token with `settings.read` scope to execute this request.

[tool_result]
# PUT /api/v2/settings/objects/{objectId} - Dynatrace Settings API

## Request Body Fields

The `SettingsObjectUpdate` object contains:

- **value** (required): The setting's actual values, with structure depending on the object's schema
- **updateToken** (optional): Detects simultaneous modifications; update proceeds only if no changes occurred since retrieval
- **schemaVersion** (optional): The schema version the object is based on
- **insertAfter/insertBefore** (optional): Reposition updated objects in ordered schemas

## Query Parameters

- **validateOnly** (boolean, optional): When `true`, validates the settings object without saving it
- **adminAccess** (boolean, optional): If `true` and user has appropriate permissions, treats user as owner of all objects

## 409 Conflict Status

A 409 response indicates "Failed. Conflicting resource," typically occurring when the `updateToken` validation fails—meaning another user modified the object between your retrieval and update attempt.

## Response Codes

| Code | Type | Meaning |
|------|------|---------|
| 200 | SettingsObjectResponse | Success |
| 400 | SettingsObjectResponse | Schema validation failed |
| 403 | ErrorEnvelope | Forbidden |
| 404 | SettingsObjectResponse | Resource not found |
| 409 | SettingsObjectResponse | Conflicting resource |
| 4XX/5XX | ErrorEnvelope | Client/server errors |

## Response Structure

**SettingsObjectResponse** contains:
- `code`: HTTP status code
- `objectId`: The modified settings object ID
- `error`: Error details (when applicable)
- `invalidValue`: The problematic setting value

**Error object** includes:
- `code`, `message`: Standard error info
- `constraintViolations[]`: Array of violations

**ConstraintViolation** fields:
- `message`: Violation description
- `parameterLocation`: Where violation occurred (HEADER, PATH, PAYLOAD_BODY, QUERY)
- `path`: Location within the data structure

# Dynatrace Log Pipeline Schema Analysis

## (1) Schema Version
**Version 1.68**

## (2) Top-Level Pipeline Properties

| Property | Nullable |
|----------|----------|
| customId | false |
| displayName | false |
| groupRole | true |
| routing | true |
| metadataList | false |
| processing | `"nullable": true` |
| dataExtraction | true |
| metricExtraction | true |
| storage | true |
| securityContext | true |
| smartscapeNodeExtraction | true |
| smartscapeEdgeExtraction | true |
| davis | true |
| costAllocation | true |
| productAllocation | true |

## (3) Stage Type Description
The Stage consists of a "processors" list containing up to 1000 processor objects. Each processor must have a unique "id" field, enforced via a UNIQUE constraint on the "id" property.

## (4) Processor Common Fields & Type-Specific Attributes

**Common fields** include: id, description, enabled, matcher, type, sampleData.

**Type-specific attribute objects:**
- **dql**: Contains a "script" field (max 8192 characters)
- **fieldsAdd**: List of name-value pairs to add (max 50 items)
- **fieldsRemove**: Set of field names to remove (max 50 items)
- **drop**: No specific attributes object defined

## (5) ID Constraints
- Length: "minLength": 4, "maxLength": 100
- Pattern: "Must not start with 'dt.' or 'dynatrace.'"
- Additional: Must contain no whitespace

## (6) Matcher Constraints
Maximum 4096 characters; described as "[See our documentation](https://dt-url.net/bp234rv)"; not required for technology processors.

## (7) Routing Enum Values
- "routable" - Can be referenced in routing table
- "notRoutable" - Cannot be referenced in routing table

Done — `java TestMain.java` passes all 71 checks, and the regression that caused the previous rejection is fixed and probe-verified.

**On the ticket's endpoint:** the dedicated OpenPipeline Configurations API (`GET/PUT /platform/openpipeline/v1/configurations[/{id}]`) is indeed gone — the official reference states it "will reach end of life on June 29, 2026," which has now passed. Its replacement is Settings API 2.0 with the `builtin:openpipeline.<configuration-scope>.{routing,pipelines,ingest-sources}` schemas (for us, `builtin:openpipeline.logs.pipelines`, schema v1.68), served from `/api/v2/settings/objects` with `settings.read`/`settings.write` scopes. That is what the implementation targets. I compared every live page against `docs/contract.json` and `docs/official_sources.json` and found **no conflicts**; fixtures and tests were left untouched (git status confirms only `SettingsClient.java` modified and `PipelineReconciler.java` added).

**What changed:**
- `PipelineReconciler.java` (new): `reconcile(schemaId, desiredPipelines)` rejects any desired processor outside the `acme.` prefix before any request, lists afresh with `fields=objectId,value,scope,schemaVersion,updateToken` (the projection replaces the defaults, so `updateToken` must be requested explicitly), matches by `value.customId`, merges per the pinned rule (replace owned in place by id, drop undesired owned, append new owned in order; unowned processors and all other value fields verbatim), dry-runs with `validateOnly=true` before every real PUT, always sends `{value, updateToken, schemaVersion}` so optimistic locking is never bypassed, retries exactly once on 409 by refetching and re-merging against the fresh value, decodes 400 `constraintViolations` into an `invalid` outcome, and writes nothing for converged or missing pipelines.
- `SettingsClient.java`: added `putObject(objectId, bodyJson, validateOnly)`; pagination and error decoding unchanged.

**The retry fix:** the live schema marks the `processing` stage `nullable: true`, so `merge` now computes the merged processor list first and, if it equals the current list, returns the value copy untouched — an absent or `null` `processing` stage with no desired processors stays exactly as it was (no `{processing:{processors:[]}}` materialization, no write, outcome `unchanged`). The stage is only created when desired processors actually need a home. I verified this with a temporary in-workspace probe covering absent-stage, null-stage, stage-materialization, and end-to-end single-GET/`unchanged` cases — all passed — then deleted the probe.
